notes: 20 items: 12 lifted, 8 fresh. Wnet = ΔKE problems: finding speed, distance, average force, or net work using the work-energy theorem.

items.question: State the WORK-ENERGY THEOREM.
items.expectedAnswer: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE).
items.explanation: Two marks: 'net work' + 'change in kinetic energy'. The theorem applies to any object regardless of whether forces are conservative or not.
options: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE).
The work done by gravity equals the change in potential energy.
The net work done on an object equals its change in momentum.

items.question: State the WORK-ENERGY THEOREM in symbols.
items.explanation: Two marks for the symbolic statement plus clear identification of variables.
options: W_net = mgh_f − mgh_i
W_net = ½mv² − ½mu²
W_net = m(v − u)

items.question: A 30 000 kg truck moving at 33 m·s⁻¹ enters an ascending arrester bed and decelerates to rest. State why the NET WORK done on the truck is NEGATIVE.
items.expectedAnswer: Its KE decreases (slows to rest), and W_net = ΔKE, so W_net is negative.
items.explanation: Direct application: ΔKE = KE_final − KE_initial = 0 − ½mv² < 0 ⇒ W_net < 0.
options: It moves uphill, and uphill motion always means negative work.
Its momentum decreases, so the work is negative.
Its KE decreases (slows to rest), and W_net = ΔKE, so W_net is negative.

items.question: A 30 000 kg truck enters an ascending arrester bed at 33 m·s⁻¹, incline 28°. Friction on the bed is 31 000 N. Calculate the minimum length of the bed needed to bring the truck to rest. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: W_net = ΔKE = 0 − ½(30 000)(33²) = −16 335 000 J. Forces opposing motion (up slope): friction + weight component along slope. (−31 000 − 30 000·9.8·sin28°)·d = −16 335 000. (−31 000 − 137 998)·d = −16 335 000 ⇒ d = 16 335 000 / 168 998 ≈ 96.7 m. (Marker tolerance varies — the official memo uses g = 9.8 and gives ≈ 96.7 m. The 70 m estimate is a common student mistake using a smaller incline term.)

items.question: Continuing the arrester-bed problem: the truck enters at the same speed but going DOWNHILL. Would the truck stop in a SHORTER or LONGER distance? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Longer — gravity's component now does positive work (adds KE), so friction must remove more, over more distance.
items.explanation: Friction still opposes motion (negative work). But gravity, instead of opposing motion (as on the way up), now does POSITIVE work along the slope. Net braking is weaker ⇒ longer stopping distance.
options: Longer — gravity's component now does positive work (adds KE), so friction must remove more, over more distance.
Shorter — going downhill the truck stops faster.
The same — slope direction doesn't affect stopping distance.

items.question: A 20 kg crate is pulled from rest from A up an 18° incline to point C (distance AC = 15.6 m along the slope) by a motor exerting a 96.8 N force parallel to the slope. Friction along the slope is 13.5 N. Calculate the SPEED at C. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)

An 18 kg crate slides from A (height 3 m) down a frictionless slope to B at the bottom, reaching 7.67 m·s⁻¹. From B it continues on a rough horizontal surface (friction = 40.6 N) and stops at C. Calculate the distance from B to C. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Apply W_net = ΔKE on the horizontal section: only friction does work. −40.6 × d = 0 − ½(18)(7.67²) = −529.9 J. d = 529.9/40.6 ≈ 13.05 m.

items.question: Same setup: 18 kg crate down a frictionless slope from height h, then rough horizontal from B to C with friction 40.6 N. If point A were at a LOWER height (less than 3 m), how would the distance from B to C compare? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Shorter — less height ⇒ less KE at B ⇒ less for friction to dissipate.
items.explanation: Energy conservation on the frictionless slope: KE_B = mgh. Then on the rough horizontal: f·d = KE_B. So d ∝ h. Smaller h ⇒ smaller d.
options: Longer — a lower start means the crate travels further.
Shorter — less height ⇒ less KE at B ⇒ less for friction to dissipate.
The same — friction dissipates energy at the same rate regardless of start height.

items.question: A 1250 kg demolition ball swings down from height R = 5.8 m on a chain. At the bottom it strikes a wall and embeds 0.25 m into it before stopping. Calculate the AVERAGE force the wall exerts on the ball. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Speed at bottom: ½mv² = mgh ⇒ v² = 2gR = 113.68. KE at impact = ½(1250)(113.68) ≈ 71 050 J. Work-energy on impact: −F × 0.25 = 0 − 71 050 ⇒ F = 71 050/0.25 ≈ 284 200 N.

items.question: A 0.06 kg ball is dropped to the ground, hits at 5.88 m·s⁻¹ downward, bounces, and rises to a maximum height of 0.605 m (taking 1.1 s after the bounce). Calculate the WORK done BY THE GROUND on the ball during the bounce. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Speed just after bounce: v_after = g × 1.1 = 10.78 m·s⁻¹. KE_after = ½(0.06)(10.78²) ≈ 3.486 J. KE_before = ½(0.06)(5.88²) ≈ 1.037 J. W_ground = ΔKE during contact = 3.486 − 1.037 ≈ 2.45 J. (Gravity's work during the brief contact is small; the official memo treats it as negligible.)

items.question: A 60 kg skier descends 80 m vertically from rest and reaches 35 m·s⁻¹ at the bottom. She travels 200 m along the slope. The friction loses 11 250 J of energy. Calculate the average frictional force on the skier.
A 2000 kg car starts from rest and accelerates over 400 m. The engine delivers a driving force of 5000 N; friction is 1200 N. Use the work-energy theorem to find the final speed.
A 2 kg block is pushed across a frictionless horizontal surface by a 10 N horizontal force for 4 m. Use the work-energy theorem to find its final speed (starting from rest).
items.explanation: W_net = Fd = 10 × 4 = 40 J. ΔKE = ½mv² ⇒ v² = 80/2 = 40 ⇒ v ≈ 6.32 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: A 5 kg block is moving at 8 m·s⁻¹ along a rough horizontal surface and decelerates to rest in 6 m. Use the work-energy theorem to find the magnitude of the friction force.

A 3 kg ball is thrown upward from the ground at 12 m·s⁻¹ and reaches a maximum height of 6.5 m. Using the work-energy theorem, find the work done by air resistance over the upward trip. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: W_net = ΔKE = 0 − ½(3)(144) = −216 J. W_gravity = −mgh = −3 × 9.8 × 6.5 = −191.1 J. W_air = W_net − W_gravity = −216 − (−191.1) = −24.9 J (negative, opposing motion).

items.question: A boy and a girl slide down a smooth (frictionless) water slide one after the other. The boy has GREATER mass than the girl. Which statement is CORRECT? (Both start from rest at the same height.)
options: Boy reaches the bottom faster (greater speed)
Girl reaches the bottom faster
Both reach the bottom at the same speed
Boy reaches the bottom slower because of his greater weight
items.expectedAnswer: Both reach the bottom at the same speed
items.explanation: On a frictionless slide, energy conservation gives mgh = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(2gh). Mass cancels. Equivalently, work-energy: W_gravity = mgh, ΔKE = ½mv² ⇒ same v for any mass.

items.question: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m·s⁻¹ brakes and comes to rest. The total braking force (friction) is 4000 N. Use the work-energy theorem to find the stopping distance.
A learner writes: 'W_net = ½mv − ½mu.' What's wrong with this statement?
items.expectedAnswer: KE is ½mv² (v squared), not ½mv — the velocities must be squared.
items.explanation: Common slip. ½mv would have units of kg·m/s = N·s (momentum), not joules.
options: Nothing — ½mv − ½mu is the correct theorem.
It should be ½m(v − u)² with the bracket squared.
KE is ½mv² (v squared), not ½mv — the velocities must be squared.

items.question: A 200 g (0.2 kg) tennis ball travelling horizontally at 25 m·s⁻¹ strikes a racket and rebounds horizontally at 30 m·s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.005 s. Calculate the AVERAGE force the racket exerts on the ball.
items.explanation: Take rebound direction as positive. Δv = +30 − (−25) = 55 m·s⁻¹. (This is actually impulse-momentum, but equivalent to applying work-energy with displacement during contact.) Using impulse: F_avg = m × Δv / Δt = 0.2 × 55 / 0.005 = 2200 N. (Pure work-energy form requires the contact displacement, which is not given here.)

items.question: A 10 kg sledge is pulled UP a 20° rough incline by a force of 80 N parallel to the slope through a distance of 5 m. The friction force is 15 N. Use the work-energy theorem to find the speed at the top, starting from rest. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: W_applied = 80 × 5 = 400 J. W_friction = −15 × 5 = −75 J. h = 5 sin20° ≈ 1.71 m. W_gravity = −mgh = −10 × 9.8 × 1.71 ≈ −167.6 J. W_net = 400 − 75 − 167.6 ≈ 157.4 J. ½mv² = 157.4 ⇒ v² = 31.48 ⇒ v ≈ 4.61 m·s⁻¹. (Allow 4.4–4.7 m·s⁻¹ depending on rounding.)

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_STATEMENT: Work-energy theorem statement missing 'net work' or 'change in KE'
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_SIGN_OF_NET_WORK: Wrong sign for W_net (e.g. positive when KE decreases)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_SIGN_OF_FRICTION: Treats friction work as positive instead of negative
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_FORCES_INCLINE: Forgets to include all force contributions (friction, weight component, applied)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_GRAVITY_INCLINE_SIGN: Wrong sign for gravity work on incline (up vs down the slope)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_NEGATIVE_WORK: Doesn't recognise stopping/decelerating means negative net work
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BOUNCE_KE_SIGN: Wrong sign convention for KE change across a bounce
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_KE_PROPORTIONALITY: Doesn't recognise v scales with √h (mass cancels)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_MASS_CANCELLATION: Predicts mass affects v on a frictionless slide
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_NET_WORK_SUM_SIGN: Sign error when summing positive and negative work contributions
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_KE_FORMULA: Uses ½mv instead of ½mv² for kinetic energy
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_VS_IMPULSE_CONFLATION: Mixes up work-energy theorem with impulse-momentum theorem
